title: Increasing, Decreasing, and the First Derivative Test
subject: AP Calculus AB

chunks.text: A function is increasing where f'(x) > 0 and decreasing where f'(x) < 0, because the derivative is the slope of the graph.
Where f'(x) = 0 the tangent line is horizontal, and the function momentarily pauses, which may or may not be a local extremum.
Critical points are interior values of x where f'(x) = 0 or where f'(x) is undefined while f itself is defined.
Critical points are the only candidates for local maxima and minima, since a function can only turn around where its slope is zero or undefined.
The Increasing/Decreasing Test: on any interval where f' > 0, f is increasing; on any interval where f' < 0, f is decreasing.
Because f' can only change sign at a critical point, testing one value per interval determines the sign of f' on the whole interval.
To build a sign chart for f', differentiate, find critical points, mark them on a number line, test the sign of f' in each interval, and translate to increasing or decreasing.
The First Derivative Test classifies a critical point by the sign change of f': positive to negative is a local maximum, negative to positive is a local minimum.
If f' does not change sign at a critical point, the point is neither a maximum nor a minimum, as with f(x) = x³ at x = 0.
A local maximum is where the function stops increasing and starts decreasing; a local minimum is where it stops decreasing and starts increasing.
Example: for f(x) = x⁴ − 8x², f'(x) = 4x(x − 2)(x + 2), with critical points x = −2, 0, 2.
For that function, f is decreasing on (−∞, −2), increasing on (−2, 0), decreasing on (0, 2), and increasing on (2, ∞).
For that function, x = −2 and x = 2 are local minima (value −16) and x = 0 is a local maximum (value 0).
Critical points include where f' is undefined: for f(x) = x^(2/3), f'(x) = (2/3)x^(−1/3) is undefined at x = 0, which is a minimum (a cusp).
Solving only f'(x) = 0 can miss extrema that occur where f' is undefined, so both conditions must be checked.
A zero of f' does not guarantee an extremum; a local extremum requires an actual sign change in f'.
The First Derivative Test works even at critical points where f' is undefined, as long as f is continuous there, since it only needs the sign change of f'.
On free response, a local maximum or minimum must be justified by stating that f' changes from positive to negative (or vice versa) there.
Stating only that f'(c) = 0 or describing the graph informally does not earn the justification point on the AP exam.
The reason f' > 0 forces f to increase is the Mean Value Theorem: f(b) − f(a) = f'(c)(b − a) is positive when b > a and f'(c) > 0.
The First Derivative Test finds local extrema; absolute extrema on a closed interval still require comparing with endpoint values via the Candidates Test.
Reading the sign of f' to determine the direction of f is the foundational skill for the entire analytical-applications unit.
